canonical_statement: The President of the United States is elected for a 4-year term.
linked_questions: The President of the United States is elected for how many years?
visual_treatment: Numeric badge — completes the term-length trio with Senate (6) and House (2) from the previous batch, though not formally clustered since it's a different branch.

canonical_statement: The President can serve only two terms because of the 22nd Amendment, which limits presidential power.
linked_questions: The President of the United States can serve only two terms. Why?
accepted_answer_variants: To keep the president from becoming too powerful
curation_rationale: Named and specific beats the vaguer 'too powerful' phrasing — same reasoning as picking 'The Great Compromise' over 'equal representation' in the previous batch.
visual_treatment: Reuses the balance-scale icon — another 'limiting power' fact, same visual family as the Great Compromise.

canonical_statement: If the President can no longer serve, the Vice President becomes President.
linked_questions: If the president can no longer serve, who becomes president?
accepted_answer_variants: The Vice President (of the United States)

canonical_statement: The President has the power to veto bills.
linked_questions: Name one power of the president.
curation_rationale: Chosen specifically to avoid duplicating facts 43 (signs bills), 42 (Commander in Chief), and 45 (appoints judges), all curated separately in this same batch — checked for overlap across the whole batch before picking, not just within this one fact.
visual_treatment: Paired conceptually with fact 43 as a sign/veto contrast, even though 43 is catalogued as its own icon_plain fact — see cluster note.

canonical_statement: The President is Commander in Chief of the U.S. military.
linked_questions: Who is Commander in Chief of the U.S. military?

canonical_statement: The President signs bills to become laws.
linked_questions: Who signs bills to become laws?
visual_treatment: Paired with fact 41 in the 'sign_or_veto' cluster.
Document/quill icon — an appointment is a formal, signed act.

canonical_statement: The Cabinet is one part of the executive branch.
linked_questions: The executive branch has many parts. Name one.
curation_rationale: More distinctive than 'President' (already covered extensively elsewhere) or the vaguer 'federal departments'.
visual_treatment: Reuses the stacked-books icon loosely to suggest a body of advisors/departments — imperfect fit, flagged as a placeholder pending a purpose-built icon.

canonical_statement: The President's Cabinet advises the President.
linked_questions: What does the President's Cabinet do?
accepted_answer_variants: Advises the President (of the United States)
visual_treatment: Same icon as fact 46, since they're directly related (what the Cabinet is / what it does).

canonical_statement: Secretary of State is one Cabinet-level position.
curated_answer: Secretary of State and Secretary of the Treasury
curation_rationale: Picked the two most globally recognizable roles, and Secretary of the Treasury connects directly back to the Alexander Hamilton entity hub already built — reinforcing an existing hub instead of introducing an unrelated pair.
visual_treatment: Reuses the globe/quill icon originally built for Jefferson's Secretary of State fact — same role, same icon, deliberate.

canonical_statement: The Electoral College decides who is elected president, as a compromise between popular vote and congressional selection.
linked_questions: Why is the Electoral College important?
accepted_answer_variants: It decides who is elected president.
It provides a compromise between the popular election of the president and congressional selection.
curated_answer: It decides who is elected president
curation_rationale: Simpler and more concrete than the compromise-framing answer.
visual_treatment: Reuses the balance-scale icon — a genuine conceptual fit this time (Electoral College literally is a compromise), not just a repeat for convenience.
